newsitem.title: MEXICO: Tensions rise in Mexico's Chiapas state.
newsitem.headline: Tensions rise in Mexico's Chiapas state.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-09-07

text.p: Increased military patrols have caused tensions to rise in the southern state of Chiapas after Zapatista rebels pulled out of peace talks, human rights and native groups said on Saturday.

The Zapatistas suspended talks on Monday in a move that embarrassed the Mexican government, which has been dealing with the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), a new leftist rebel force that has carried out a series of attacks that have left several dead and wounded in other states.
Humanitarian groups and native leaders said that people in the area of Ocosingo in Chiapas were on alert after various government troop movements.

The municipal council of Ocosingo, where some of the bloodiest fighting of the Zapatista uprising took place in early 1994, issued a letter to President Ernesto Zedillo, saying peace will not come until talks start again.
The mainly native-led council said in a statement that, "for no reasons must we permit that advance of the units of the federal Mexican army into the native communities."
In the roads between the state capital of Tuxtla Gutierrez and San Cristobal de Las Casas, military convoys were constantly on the move, witnesses said.
"The situation is alarming," said Carlos Rodriguez, spokesman for the Co-ordinating group of Non-governmental Organisation for Peace.
Government official played down any heightened tensions.

"Although the army has taken precautions to protect strategic installations like hydroelectric dams and fuel depots, in the disputed zone military movements in the last few days were routine patrols to supply military bases," said Uriel Jarquin, a Chiapas state government official.
However, some native leaders said that some small villages were surrounded by troops, which increased tensions.
The Zapatistas said that the government has taken advantage of the unrest caused by the EPR to crack down on Zapatista supporters.

In April 1995 the Zaptista rebels and government envoys agreed to relaunch peace talks in the Chiapas village of San Andres Larrainzar. They have reached an accord on indigenous rights, but other issues remain outstanding.
